---
title: "Neighbourhood covariates"
subtitle: "An experiment: ten Census 2021 measures of diversity, migration, deprivation and work, added one at a time to Value Added v2.1. Do they explain the place effects, or something else?"
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site_helpers.R"))
N <- readRDS(here::here("data", "neighbourhood_covariates.rds"))
R <- N$res
r1 <- function(g, m, col) R[[col]][R$group == g & R$model == m]
cf <- function(g, m, term) { x <- R$coefs[[which(R$group == g & R$model == m)]]; 100 * (exp(x$est[x$term == term]) - 1) }
ctt <- function(g, m, term) { x <- R$coefs[[which(R$group == g & R$model == m)]]; x$est[x$term == term] / x$se[x$term == term] }
SO <- "School's own White British share"
p1 <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f%%", x)
GCOL <- c("All pupils" = LPURPLE, "Disadvantaged pupils" = DPURPLE)
T2 <- readRDS(here::here("data", "graduate_deprivation.rds"))
tres <- function(g, s) T2$res[T2$res$group == g & T2$res$spec == s, ]
tc <- function(g, s, term, col = "pct") { x <- tres(g, s)$coefs[[1]]; x <- x[x$term == term, ]
  if (col == "t") x$est / x$se else 100 * (exp(x$est) - 1) }
kv <- function(g, k, m) T2$kind_va$va[T2$kind_va$group == g & T2$kind_va$kind == k & T2$kind_va$model == m]
kd <- function(k, col) T2$kinds[[col]][T2$kinds$kind == k]
DG <- "Deprived, many graduates"; DF <- "Deprived, few graduates"
PL <- "+ deprivation by kind of place"; EC <- "+ deprivation and early-career measures"; PT <- "Deprivation in parts"
PN <- readRDS(here::here("data", "parents_not_adults.rds"))
pv <- function(g, s, col) PN$cmp[[col]][PN$cmp$group == g & PN$cmp$spec == s]
pcf <- function(g, s, term) { x <- PN$cmp$coefs[[which(PN$cmp$group == g & PN$cmp$spec == s)]]; 100 * (exp(x$est[x$term == term]) - 1) }
pkv <- function(g, k, m) PN$kv$va[PN$kv$group == g & PN$kv$kind == k & PN$kv$model == m]
pg <- function(k, col) PN$gap[[col]][PN$gap$kind == k]
st <- function(g, s, term, col = "pct") PN$split_test[[col]][PN$split_test$group == g & PN$split_test$sample == s & PN$split_test$term == term]
```

::: {.callout-note}
## An experiment, not a change to the model

Value Added v2.1 is unchanged. This page tests candidate terms, on the
same school-years and the same specification, to see what they would do.
Everything is published data: Census 2021 tables for Output Areas and
the January 2026 school census.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## In short

- **The largest gain is not a place measure.** It is the school's own share of White British pupils, which v2.1 does not have. For disadvantaged pupils, one standard deviation more goes with `r p1(r1("disadvantaged", SO, "pct"))` Attainment 8, all else equal. Once it is in, the neighbourhood's ethnic make-up adds little: what looked like a neighbourhood effect was mostly who the pupils are.
- **Neighbourhood deprivation, beyond qualifications, does matter.** At the same share of graduates, more multiply deprived households around a school go with *higher* results for disadvantaged pupils. This survives the school's own composition.
- **Together they take a fifth off the local authority effects for disadvantaged pupils, and over a third off the regional ones.** For all pupils, authority effects barely change.
- **About a third of Brighton and Hove's effect goes with these measures.** Its neighbourhoods are more deprived than their graduate share suggests.
:::

## The measures {#sec-measures}

Each is built exactly as neighbourhood education is: the average over the
`r N$k` Output Areas nearest each school, standardised across schools.

| Measure | Census 2021 table |
|---|---|
| White British (%); ethnic diversity (the chance two residents are from different groups, across 19) | TS021 |
| Born outside the UK (%) | TS004 |
| Cannot speak English well or at all (%) | TS029 |
| Arrived from abroad in the last year (%) | TS019 |
| Households deprived in two or more of four dimensions: employment, education, health, housing (%) | TS011 |
| Social renting (%) | TS054 |
| Routine, semi-routine or never worked (%); higher professional (%) | TS062 |
| Lone parents with dependent children (%) | TS003 |

Several move together closely. White British and born outside the UK
correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", N$cors["z_wbri", "z_born_abroad"])`.
Higher professional correlates with neighbourhood education at
`r sprintf("%.2f", N$cors["z_l4", "z_higher_prof"])`, and routine work
with it at `r sprintf("%.2f", N$cors["z_l4", "z_routine"])`. So read the
measures in families, not one by one. To these is added the **school's own
share of White British pupils** (January 2026 census). It is a pupil
measure, not a neighbourhood one, and v2.1 has no pupil ethnicity, only
English as an additional language.

## One at a time {#sec-one}

```{r}
#| label: fig-one
#| fig-cap: "Each measure added on its own to the v2.1 model: the difference in Attainment 8 with one standard deviation more (%), with 95% intervals, for all pupils and disadvantaged pupils. Maximum likelihood, the same school-years throughout."
#| fig-height: 5.6
one <- R |> filter(n_terms == 1) |>
  mutate(grp = ifelse(group == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged pupils"),
         lo = 100 * (exp(est - 1.96 * se) - 1), hi = 100 * (exp(est + 1.96 * se) - 1))
lev <- one |> filter(group == "disadvantaged") |> arrange(pct) |> pull(model)
ggplot(one |> mutate(model = factor(model, lev)), aes(pct, model, colour = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% difference in Attainment 8 per standard deviation", y = NULL) + theme_note(11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

For all pupils every effect is small: about one per cent per standard
deviation at most. For disadvantaged pupils they are three to five times
larger. Disadvantaged pupils do better around schools in diverse,
migrant, less English-speaking and more deprived neighbourhoods, and
worse in White British and professional ones. The school's own White
British share is the strongest single term:
`r p1(r1("disadvantaged", SO, "pct"))` for disadvantaged pupils and
`r p1(r1("all", SO, "pct"))` for all.

## Composition or place? {#sec-composition}

A neighbourhood's ethnic make-up and a school's pupils go together. The
question is whether the neighbourhood matters *beyond* who the pupils
are. With the school's own White British share in the model:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-comp
#| tbl-cap: "The school's own White British share with neighbourhood measures alongside: each term's effect (% per SD, with its t value), for disadvantaged pupils and all pupils."
mods <- c("School's own + neighbourhood White British", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation")
terms <- c(z_sch_wbri = "School's own White British share", z_wbri = "Neighbourhood White British",
           z_deprived2 = "Neighbourhood deprivation (2+ dimensions)")
bind_rows(lapply(mods, function(m) bind_rows(lapply(c("disadvantaged", "all"), function(g) {
  x <- R$coefs[[which(R$group == g & R$model == m)]]
  tibble(Model = m, Group = ifelse(g == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged"), Term = terms[x$term],
         `% per SD` = sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (exp(x$est) - 1)), t = sprintf("%.1f", x$est / x$se))
})))) |>
  kt(align = "lllrr") |> kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, valign = "top")
```

- **Ethnicity is mostly composition.** With the school's own share in, the neighbourhood's White British share shrinks from `r p1(r1("disadvantaged", "White British (%)", "pct"))` to `r p1(cf("disadvantaged", mods[1], "z_wbri"))` for disadvantaged pupils, and to nothing clear for all pupils (`r p1(cf("all", mods[1], "z_wbri"))`, t `r sprintf("%.1f", ctt("all", mods[1], "z_wbri"))`). The model fits barely better with both than with the school's own share alone (AIC `r sprintf("%.0f", r1("disadvantaged", mods[1], "aic_change"))` against `r sprintf("%.0f", r1("disadvantaged", SO, "aic_change"))`).
- **Deprivation is place.** Neighbourhood deprivation keeps its effect alongside the school's composition: `r p1(cf("disadvantaged", mods[2], "z_deprived2"))` per SD for disadvantaged pupils (t `r sprintf("%.1f", ctt("disadvantaged", mods[2], "z_deprived2"))`) and `r p1(cf("all", mods[2], "z_deprived2"))` for all. At the same share of graduates and the same pupils, a school in a more multiply deprived neighbourhood does a little better. The next section asks why.

## Two kinds of deprived neighbourhood {#sec-two}

Why would more deprivation, at the same share of graduates, go with better
results? One idea is that this is the inner city, near universities and
above all London: neighbourhoods full of recent graduates who are
culturally and educationally rich but not yet financially so, unlike
deprived towns without graduate jobs. The geography is right. The schools
in the top third of England for neighbourhood deprivation split into two
very different kinds of place:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kinds
#| tbl-cap: "Schools in the top third for neighbourhood deprivation, by whether they are also in the top or bottom third for neighbourhood education, 2024/25. Neighbourhoods are the 150 nearest Output Areas; 'near a university' is within 5 km of a higher education institution's registered address."
rows <- c(schools = "Schools", london = "In London (%)", near_uni = "Near a university (%)", young = "Aged 25 to 34 (%)",
          private_rent = "Private renting (%)", overcrowd = "Overcrowded households (%)", bad_health = "Bad or very bad health (%)",
          lt_sick = "Long-term sick or disabled (%)", l4 = "Adults with degree-level qualifications (%)",
          fsm = "Disadvantaged pupils (FSM6, %)", wbri = "White British pupils (%)")
tibble(` ` = unname(rows),
       `Deprived, many graduates` = sapply(names(rows), function(v) format(round(kd(DG, v), ifelse(v == "schools", 0, 1)), nsmall = ifelse(v == "schools", 0, 1))),
       `Deprived, few graduates` = sapply(names(rows), function(v) format(round(kd(DF, v), ifelse(v == "schools", 0, 1)), nsmall = ifelse(v == "schools", 0, 1)))) |>
  kt(align = "lrr")
```

Deprived neighbourhoods with many graduates are
`r round(kd(DG, "london"))`% London, and `r round(kd(DG, "near_uni"))`% are
near a university. They are young, privately rented and overcrowded.
Deprived neighbourhoods with few graduates are almost none of those; they
are older and sicker. The authorities with most such schools are
`r paste(head(T2$top_las$LANAME[T2$top_las$kind == DG], 3), collapse = ", ")`,
against `r paste(head(T2$top_las$LANAME[T2$top_las$kind == DF], 3), collapse = ", ")`.

**Disadvantaged pupils do far better in the first kind, but most of that is
who they are.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-kinds
#| fig-cap: "Average value added against England (% of Attainment 8, with one standard error) by kind of neighbourhood: under v2.1, with the school's own ethnicity allowed for, and with neighbourhood deprivation too. Top and bottom thirds of schools on neighbourhood deprivation and neighbourhood education."
#| fig-height: 4.6
KV <- T2$kind_va |> filter(group != "all") |>
  mutate(grp = ifelse(group == "disadvantaged", "Disadvantaged pupils", "Non-disadvantaged pupils"),
         model = factor(model, c("v2.1", "+ school's ethnicity", "+ ethnicity and deprivation")),
         kind = factor(kind, rev(c(DG, DF, "Not deprived, many graduates", "Not deprived, few graduates"))))
ggplot(KV, aes(va, kind, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = va - se, xmax = va + se), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ grp) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("v2.1" = MPURPLE, "+ school's ethnicity" = BPURPLE, "+ ethnicity and deprivation" = DPURPLE), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) ifelse(x == 0, "0%", paste0(sprintf("%+.0f", x), "%"))) +
  labs(x = "Value added against England, % of Attainment 8", y = NULL) + theme_note(11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Under v2.1, disadvantaged pupils in deprived, graduate-rich neighbourhoods
are `r p1(kv("disadvantaged", DG, "v2.1"))` above expectation, and in deprived,
low-graduate ones `r p1(kv("disadvantaged", DF, "v2.1"))`. The schools in the
first group have `r round(kd(DG, "wbri"))`% White British pupils, against
`r round(kd(DF, "wbri"))`% in the second. With that allowed for, the lead falls to
`r p1(kv("disadvantaged", DG, "+ school's ethnicity"))`: two-thirds of it is
composition. The rest is real but modest.

Does the graduate idea explain the deprivation effect itself? It makes four
predictions, and the data support it only in part:

| If it is recent graduates, the deprivation effect should... | What the data show |
|---|---|
| grow with neighbourhood education | **No.** The interaction is `r sprintf("%+.2f", tc("disadvantaged", "+ deprivation x neighbourhood education", "z_l4:z_dep"))`% for disadvantaged pupils and `r sprintf("%+.2f", tc("non_disadvantaged", "+ deprivation x neighbourhood education", "z_l4:z_dep"))`% for non-disadvantaged (the wrong way) |
| sit in London and near universities, not in low-graduate places | **In part.** For disadvantaged pupils it is `r p1(tc("disadvantaged", PL, "place4London:z_dep"))` in London and `r p1(tc("disadvantaged", PL, "place4Near a university:z_dep"))` near universities, but also `r p1(tc("disadvantaged", PL, "place4Elsewhere, fewer graduates:z_dep"))` in low-graduate places. For non-disadvantaged pupils it is largest in low-graduate places (`r p1(tc("non_disadvantaged", PL, "place4Elsewhere, fewer graduates:z_dep"))`) |
| go once early-career measures are in | **No.** It stays at `r p1(tc("disadvantaged", EC, "z_dep"))` for disadvantaged pupils and rises to `r p1(tc("non_disadvantaged", EC, "z_dep"))` for non-disadvantaged |
| be overcrowding, not ill health | **In part.** Overcrowding is positive for disadvantaged pupils (`r p1(tc("disadvantaged", PT, "z_overcrowd"))`), but so is bad health (`r p1(tc("disadvantaged", PT, "z_bad_health"))`) |

So the small deprivation term is not a recent-graduate effect. It appears in
both kinds of place, for reasons this page cannot separate.

**But the graduates may matter in a different way.** Two results point the
same way. In deprived, graduate-rich neighbourhoods, *non-disadvantaged* pupils
do worse than expected (`r p1(kv("non_disadvantaged", DG, "v2.1"))`). And at the same
share of graduates, more young adults go with slightly lower results for
every group (`r p1(tc("all", EC, "z_young"))` for all pupils). A likely reading
is that many recent graduates are not the pupils' parents. Neighbourhood
education counts every adult, so young and often childless graduates raise
it, and v2.1 then expects more of the local schools than their families
warrant. The next section tests that directly.

## Parents, not adults {#sec-parents}

Neighbourhood education counts every adult. Custom Census 2021 tables from
ONS allow something closer to the pupils' families: **level 4+ qualifications
among adults aged 25 to 64 in households with dependent children**, published
by MSOA, the finest level available. Limiting the age leaves out 16 to 18 year
olds who are themselves dependent children. Each measure is averaged over a
school's same `r N$k` nearest Output Areas, and all adults are rebuilt at MSOA
level too, so differences are about who is counted, not the coarser map.

**The measure is distorted where the idea says it should be.**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Share with level 4+ qualifications around schools, by kind of neighbourhood: all adults, adults aged 25 to 64 with and without dependent children in the household."
PN$gap |> mutate(k = factor(kind, c(DG, DF, "Not deprived, many graduates", "Not deprived, few graduates"))) |> arrange(k) |>
  transmute(Neighbourhood = kind, Schools = schools, `All adults` = sprintf("%.1f%%", all_msoa),
            `Parents` = sprintf("%.1f%%", parents), `Adults without dependent children` = sprintf("%.1f%%", nonpar)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

Deprived, graduate-rich neighbourhoods and comfortable graduate-rich ones look
identical on all adults (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", pg(DG, "all_msoa"))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", pg("Not deprived, many graduates", "all_msoa"))`). Among
parents they are `r round(pg("Not deprived, many graduates", "parents") - pg(DG, "parents"))`
points apart (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", pg(DG, "parents"))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", pg("Not deprived, many graduates", "parents"))`). In the first,
adults without children are the graduates; in the second, parents are.

**Measuring parents explains two of the three puzzles.**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-puzzles
#| tbl-cap: "What changes when neighbourhood education is measured among parents instead of all adults. The effects (% per SD) come from models that also allow for the school's ethnicity, neighbourhood deprivation and young adults; the last row is value added against England with only the neighbourhood term swapped."
A1 <- "All adults + ethnicity, deprivation, young adults"; P1 <- "Parents + ethnicity, deprivation, young adults"
GR <- c("all", "disadvantaged", "non_disadvantaged", "girls", "boys")
tibble(Result = c("Young adults' effect, all pupils", "Young adults' effect, non-disadvantaged", "Young adults' effect, boys",
                  "Neighbourhood deprivation's effect, all pupils", "Neighbourhood deprivation's effect, disadvantaged",
                  "Non-disadvantaged pupils in deprived, graduate-rich places"),
       `All adults` = c(p1(pcf("all", A1, "z_young")), p1(pcf("non_disadvantaged", A1, "z_young")), p1(pcf("boys", A1, "z_young")),
                        p1(pcf("all", A1, "z_dep")), p1(pcf("disadvantaged", A1, "z_dep")), p1(pkv("non_disadvantaged", DG, "All adults"))),
       Parents = c(p1(pcf("all", P1, "z_young")), p1(pcf("non_disadvantaged", P1, "z_young")), p1(pcf("boys", P1, "z_young")),
                   p1(pcf("all", P1, "z_dep")), p1(pcf("disadvantaged", P1, "z_dep")), p1(pkv("non_disadvantaged", DG, "Parents")))) |>
  kt(align = "lrr")
```

The penalty for young adults almost disappears, and so does the shortfall for
non-disadvantaged pupils in deprived, graduate-rich places. Those were
artefacts of counting adults who are not parents. **The deprivation effect
does not go.** It is not a by-product of the qualification term, for any group.

**But parents alone are not a better term.** Used in place of all adults,
parents improve the model for non-disadvantaged pupils and make it slightly
worse for the other four groups. Both together are better for all five.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pfit
#| tbl-cap: "Against v2.1, by group: the change in AIC and in out-of-sample error (each year predicted from the other three) with parents in place of all adults, and with parents and adults without dependent children both in."
SP <- "Parents (MSOA)"; SB <- "Parents and non-parents together"; S0 <- "v2.1: all adults (Output Areas)"
tibble(Group = unname(GROUP_LABELS[GR]),
       `Parents: AIC` = sapply(GR, function(g) sprintf("%+.0f", pv(g, SP, "aic_change"))),
       `Parents: error` = sapply(GR, function(g) sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * (pv(g, SP, "rmse_oos") / pv(g, S0, "rmse_oos") - 1))),
       `Both: AIC` = sapply(GR, function(g) sprintf("%+.0f", pv(g, SB, "aic_change"))),
       `Both: error` = sapply(GR, function(g) sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * (pv(g, SB, "rmse_oos") / pv(g, S0, "rmse_oos") - 1)))) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

**With both in, the two groups of pupils respond to different graduates.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-split
#| fig-cap: "The effect of graduates among parents and among adults without dependent children, entered together with the school's ethnicity, % of Attainment 8 per SD with 95% intervals, for England, outside London and London."
#| fig-height: 3.8
sp <- tibble::as_tibble(PN$split_test) |> filter(sample %in% c("England", "Outside London", "London"), term != "z_eth", group != "all") |>
  mutate(grp = ifelse(group == "disadvantaged", "Disadvantaged pupils", "Non-disadvantaged pupils"),
         who = ifelse(term == "z_parents", "Graduates among parents", "Graduates among adults without dependent children"),
         sample = factor(sample, rev(c("England", "Outside London", "London"))),
         lo = 100 * (exp(est - 1.96 * se) - 1), hi = 100 * (exp(est + 1.96 * se) - 1))
ggplot(sp, aes(pct, sample, colour = who)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 2.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ grp) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Graduates among parents" = DPURPLE, "Graduates among adults without dependent children" = BLUE), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% of Attainment 8 per SD", y = NULL) + theme_note(11) + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

- **Non-disadvantaged pupils' results follow graduate parents**
  (`r p1(st("non_disadvantaged", "England", "z_parents"))`, t `r sprintf("%.1f", st("non_disadvantaged", "England", "z_parents", "t"))`).
  Other graduates nearby add nothing clear
  (`r p1(st("non_disadvantaged", "England", "z_nonpar"))`). This holds inside and
  outside London. It is what a measure of family background should do.
- **Disadvantaged pupils do better near graduates who are not parents**
  (`r p1(st("disadvantaged", "England", "z_nonpar"))`, t `r sprintf("%.1f", st("disadvantaged", "England", "z_nonpar", "t"))`), and a little
  worse near graduate parents (`r p1(st("disadvantaged", "England", "z_parents"))`).
  That appears in London and outside it, so it is not simply a London effect.
  It is smaller than it first looks: about 60% of the split goes once the
  school's ethnicity is allowed for, and outside London the parents' side is
  no longer clear.

The second result fits the idea that young graduates bring something to a
neighbourhood that reaches disadvantaged pupils. It fits other stories too.
Disadvantaged pupils among graduate parents may be more isolated, or more
disadvantaged within their school. The two measures also overlap heavily
(correlation `r sprintf("%.2f", PN$cors["z_parents", "z_nonpar"])`), so the
split rests on the places where they differ. It is an association to follow
up, not a finding about cause.

**For the model.** Neighbourhood deprivation survives with parents measured
properly, so the case for it in v2.2 stands. Splitting neighbourhood education
into parents and other adults would help every group a little, and is a
further candidate. Parents here means adults aged 25 to 64 in a household with
a dependent child, which also takes in some grandparents and older siblings,
at MSOA level.

## Do they explain the place effects? {#sec-place}

```{r}
#| label: fig-place
#| fig-cap: "How much the local authority and region variances change when each set of terms is added (%). Negative: the terms account for part of what the authority or region effects were picking up."
#| fig-height: 4.8
SETS_SHOW <- c("Diversity and migration", "Deprivation and work", "All ten", SO,
               "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation", "School's own + all ten")
pl <- R |> filter(model %in% SETS_SHOW) |>
  select(group, model, `Local authority` = la_var_change, Region = reg_var_change) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(`Local authority`, Region), names_to = "level", values_to = "chg") |>
  mutate(grp = ifelse(group == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged pupils"), model = factor(model, rev(SETS_SHOW)))
ggplot(pl, aes(chg, model, fill = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ level) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GCOL, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(sprintf("%+.0f", x), "%")) +
  labs(x = "Change in variance (%)", y = NULL) + theme_note(11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

For **disadvantaged pupils**, the school's composition with neighbourhood
deprivation takes `r sprintf("%.0f", -r1("disadvantaged", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation", "la_var_change"))`%
off the local authority variance and
`r sprintf("%.0f", -r1("disadvantaged", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation", "reg_var_change"))`%
off the regional variance. Part of why disadvantaged pupils do better in
London and some cities than in the South East or coastal towns is who the
pupils are and what their neighbourhoods are like, at the same intake
otherwise.

For **all pupils**, authority effects barely change and regional ones
grow. The measures account for differences *within* regions, which leaves
the differences between them larger. For most pupils, what makes an
authority's schools do better is not in these measures.

## Brighton and Hove {#sec-bh}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bh
#| tbl-cap: "Brighton and Hove's local authority effect (% of Attainment 8) in the v2.1 model and with terms added."
bm <- c("Baseline (v2.1)", SO, "Households deprived in 2+ dimensions (%)", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation",
        "School's own + deprivation and work", "School's own + all ten")
R |> filter(model %in% bm) |> select(group, model, bh) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = bh) |>
  mutate(m = factor(model, bm)) |> arrange(m) |>
  transmute(Model = model, `All pupils` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", all), Disadvantaged = sprintf("%+.1f%%", disadvantaged)) |>
  kt(align = "lrr")
```

Brighton and Hove's effect is one of the largest in England
([its own page](bh_effect.qmd)). Its schools' pupils are mostly White
British, so adding the school's composition, if anything, *raises* the
effect. Neighbourhood deprivation and work lower it, from
`r p1(r1("all", "Baseline (v2.1)", "bh"))` to
`r p1(r1("all", "School's own + deprivation and work", "bh"))` for all
pupils, and from `r p1(r1("disadvantaged", "Baseline (v2.1)", "bh"))` to
`r p1(r1("disadvantaged", "School's own + deprivation and work", "bh"))` for
disadvantaged pupils. The city's neighbourhoods have many graduates, but
also more households deprived on the Census measures than that suggests. Neighbourhood
education alone makes them look more advantaged than they are. About a
third of the effect goes with that; the rest is still unexplained.

## What it means for the model {#sec-means}

- **A candidate for v2.2: pupils' ethnicity.** DfE's contextual value
  added, in the performance tables until 2011, included pupils' ethnicity. Progress 8 does not,
  and nor does v2.1. The evidence here is that leaving it out matters most
  for disadvantaged pupils. Whether to put it in is a question of what the
  measure is for. Adjusting for it would stop schools with many White
  British disadvantaged pupils looking worse for it. It would also take a
  real difference in results out of view. It belongs with the review's
  other recommendations.
- **A candidate for neighbourhood: deprivation beside education.** Adding
  household deprivation to neighbourhood education improves the model for
  every group. It is not specific to graduate-rich places
  ([above](#sec-two)), and a measure of parents' qualifications may do
  the job better.
- **What is left of place.** Even with all of it, most of the local
  authority effects remain, especially for all pupils. What makes some
  authorities' schools do better than their intakes predict is not in the
  Census.

## How it was done {#sec-how}

Each model is the full v2.1 specification for its group, with the same
random effects for year and region/local authority, fitted by maximum
likelihood so that AIC can be compared. Every fit uses the same
`r format(r1("all", "Baseline (v2.1)", "rows"), big.mark = ",")` school-years for all pupils and
`r format(r1("disadvantaged", "Baseline (v2.1)", "rows"), big.mark = ",")` for disadvantaged pupils
(those with every measure). The school's own White British share is from
January 2026 and is used for every year, since earlier school census files
in the performance tables do not include ethnicity. Neighbourhoods are
the `r N$k` nearest Output Areas to the school, not pupils' homes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-all
#| tbl-cap: "Every model: the change in AIC against v2.1 (negative is better), and in the local authority and region variances."
R |> filter(model != "Baseline (v2.1)") |>
  transmute(Group = ifelse(group == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged"), Model = model,
            `% per SD` = ifelse(is.na(pct), "", sprintf("%+.2f", pct)), `AIC change` = sprintf("%.0f", aic_change),
            `Authority variance` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", la_var_change), `Region variance` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", reg_var_change)) |>
  kt(align = "llrrrr") |> kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top") |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "420px")
```
